title: The Pacific Arbitrage
summary:
The Pacific Arbitrage
When considering the current clean market it is difficult not to notice the development of new trade patterns that have emerged over the past several years. In addition to these new trade routes the more established routes have been seeing more traffic. The primary drivers in this evolution have been the regional supply and demand imbalances of clean refined products and the resulting price arbitrages.

children.title: Total Reported Tons Fixed
children.summary: Annualized Projection It is anticipated that strong demand for high quality refined products will continue on the US West Coast, but there is uncertainty as to how long the price arbitrage window will remain. According to the EIA, total imports for gasoline, diesel and kerosene topped 8.6 million tons for the first 11 months of 2006, which equates to nearly 250 Handymax parcels.

children.title: Paying Their Way
children.summary: At current market levels, transportation costs roughly $41 per metric ton. While the freight market certainly has its swings, when compared to the product price market, freight looks relatively steady.

children.title: Charterers' Transportation Costs
children.summary: Diesel Gasoline For the first three quarters of 2006, the arbitrage did not support the transportation of diesel on this trade, while the price disparity for gasoline tended to stay above freight costs justifying movement. What is most interesting, however, is how prices have been structured so far in 2007.

children.title: The Regulation Wrinkle
children.summary: A pervasive obstacle throughout several markets, and in particular the US West Coast, has been changing environmental regulations. The data above suggests that at the time of the switch to ultra-low sulfur diesel in mid-October of 2006, refiners were unable to bring enough product to market in order to satisfy demand.
